newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's biggest casino opens doors to Asia.
newsitem.headline: Australia's biggest casino opens doors to Asia.

text.p: Asia's largest casino and hotel complex, Crown casino, opens its doors in Australia on Thursday, betting the region's high rollers will repay its enormous cost.
The Melbourne complex, costed by some analysts at over A$2 billion (US$1.56 billion), dwarfs Australia's 13 other casinos and has worried investors as well as anti-gambling crusaders.

"At the moment the (share) market is very keen to see Crown demonstrate the investment in the casino has been a good one, that it generates the returns that support the huge investment," a Sydney-based analyst told Reuters on Tuesday.
Apart from the casino, the Crown Entertainment Complex will house Australia's largest hotel, a convention centre, a cinema complex, 52 bars and restaurants and 34 upmarket retailers.
The entire complex on the banks of Melbourne's Yarra River has been designed with Asian tastes in mind.
"The focus at the moment is Asia in terms of international revenue," Crown Ltd chairman and founder Lloyd Williams said in promotional material handed out on the eve of the opening.
Asian gamblers have accounted for about a third of revenue from the casino's old premises, a minnow compared with its replacement. Crown now hopes to take this to over 60 percent.
Crown's success with Asian gamblers has underpinned its record as the most profitable of Australia's casinos, but its winning streak has not been unbroken.

Crown's shares fell sharply in mid-January after it revealed that capital cost estimates had ballooned to A$1.55 billion from its previous estimate of A$1.25 billion. It originally planned in its prospectus to spend about A$550 million.
Sceptics have nicknamed the new complex the "Spruce Goose", after the U.S.-made 1940s seaplane that was too big to fly.
But share analysts believe Crown will pocket revenues of over A$1 billion in its first year in the new complex.
Investors have pinned their faith on Williams, the company's driving force. He is also chief executive of Hudson Conway Ltd, which manages the casino and owns about 31 percent of Crown.
Inspired by the glittering casino palaces of Las Vegas, Williams is aggressively tempting Asian high rollers. He sees them as pivotal to Crown's success.
Crown has set up Asian marketing offices in Singapore, Hong Kong, Bangkok, Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur and Taipei and plans to open two offices in China.
Crown won the exclusive casino licence for Victoria state in September 1993 and has operated a temporary casino since June 1994. Last year, the old casino reaped A$557 million in revenue.
The project's fiercest critics have come from outside the share market.

Church and welfare groups argue the new casino will magnify existing gambling problems, while local retailers see it as a serious threat to their earnings. One in every 30 dollars earned in Victoria state is already spent on gambling.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard has also frowned on the proliferation of gambling. He has said he believes gambling has reached saturation point.
Howard, who will not attend the casino opening in favour of another engagement, has voiced concerns about the impact of gambling on the poor and on small business. (A$1 = US$0.78)
